page.h1: HTS Chapter 22: Beverages, Spirits and Vinegar — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Exporting Alcohol from the U.S.: Schedule B, TTB Tax-Free Export & Certificates (HTS Ch. 22) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What the U.S. requires to export bourbon, wine, beer and ethanol: Schedule B codes, TTB tax-free removal and drawback, TTB export certificates and EU VI-1, the Russia licence, EPA RINs.
keywords: how to export alcohol from usa

intro: Exporting beverages and spirits is mostly a **TTB** matter on the U.S. side. Bourbon, other spirits, wine and beer can leave a distillery, winery or brewery **without paying federal excise tax** when they are exported, on a TTB form for each shipment, with the cases marked “Export” and proof of export kept; if the tax was already paid, TTB refunds it as drawback. TTB also issues the **export certificates** buyers ask for, such as certificates of origin and age, the bourbon certificate of authenticity and the EU’s VI-1 for wine. Commerce licences rarely apply: drinks and ethanol are EAR99, except that beer, wine, spirits and undenatured ethanol need a licence for Russia and Belarus. Fuel ethanol exporters must also retire Renewable Fuel Standard credits (RINs) for the volume they ship, and soft drinks, water and vinegar are FDA foods, for which FDA issues export certificates on request.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Bourbon is 2208.30.6020 (containers of 4 liters or less) or 2208.30.6040 (over 4 liters); other whiskies are 2208.30.9025–9040. Fuel ethanol is 2207.10.6010 (undenatured) or 2207.20.0010 (denatured). Still wine in bottles is under 2204.21, beer 2203.00.0000, vodka 2208.60.0000, soft drinks 2202.10 and 2202.99. Spirits are reported in proof liters, wine, beer and ethanol in liters.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Beverages, spirits and ethanol are EAR99: no Commerce licence is needed for most destinations. Russia and Belarus are the exception (see the sanctions step).

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: Alcoholic beverages are not food or medicine for the humanitarian permissions in most programs. For Russia and Belarus, BIS treats beer, wine, spirits and undenatured ethanol as luxury goods that need a licence (15 CFR 746.8(a)(7)).

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: A tank car or vessel of ethanol, or a container of spirits or wine, is almost always over $2,500 per Schedule B number. Shipments to Canada, the largest buyer, are exempt from EEI filing unless they need a licence or move on through Canada to a third country (15 CFR 30.36). TTB keeps its own proof-of-export rule for tax-free alcohol: the export bill of lading or a carrier certificate (27 CFR 28.40).

rules.agency: Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB)
rules.title: Ship spirits, wine and beer out without paying federal excise tax. For distilled spirits (including bourbon and undenatured ethanol), the distilled spirits plant or a wholesaler files TTB F 5100.11 for each shipment, and TTB must approve it before the goods leave bonded premises (27 CFR 28.91–28.92); wine follows the same form (27 CFR 28.121–28.122), and a brewer files a notice on TTB F 5130.12 (27 CFR 28.141–28.142). Specially denatured spirits can also be withdrawn free of tax for export (27 CFR 28.151). Each case or barrel is marked "Export" (27 CFR 28.103, 28.123, 28.144), and the exporter must keep evidence of exportation, such as a copy of the export bill of lading or a certificate by the export carrier (27 CFR 28.40–28.43); without it the tax becomes due.

citations.label: TTB: exporting distilled spirits without payment of tax

rules.agency: Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB)
rules.title: Federal excise tax back on taxpaid alcohol you export: if the tax was already paid, the bottler of spirits files TTB F 5110.30 and gets drawback equal to the tax paid once TTB receives proof of export (27 CFR 28.171, 28.190); wine uses TTB F 5120.24 (27 CFR 28.211, 28.214) and beer TTB F 5130.6 (27 CFR 28.221–28.222). This is a refund of U.S. excise tax, separate from Customs duty drawback on imported inputs.

citations.label: TTB: exporters of taxpaid distilled spirits

rules.agency: Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB)
rules.title: Wholesaler's basic permit: anyone other than a qualified distilled spirits plant who goes into the business of exporting distilled spirits must first hold a basic permit under the Federal Alcohol Administration Act (27 CFR Part 1), applied for through TTB Permits Online.

citations.label: TTB: exporting distilled spirits without payment of tax

rules.agency: Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB), International Affairs Division
rules.title: Export certificates the buyer's country asks for. TTB is not required by law to issue them but does, electronically in myTTB since July 18, 2023 or on its paper templates: certificates of free sale, origin and/or age, health, sanitation and authenticity. For spirits, TTB F 5110.58 is the Certificate of Origin and Age (27 CFR 28.104) and TTB F 5110.42 the Certificate of Authenticity for Bourbon Whisky. U.S. wine shipped to the EU needs either the self-certified EU simplified export certificate or a VI-1 form for each lot; China accepts a consolidated wine certificate; other APEC economies use the APEC Model Wine Certificate; Brazil wants separate certificates of origin and of analysis (analysis by a TTB-certified laboratory).

Renewable Fuel Standard: an exporter of fuel ethanol, neat or blended, must acquire and retire enough RINs to cover the exported volume (its Exporter Renewable Volume Obligation), unless it bought the fuel directly from the producer and can show no RINs were generated (40 CFR 80.1430).

rules.agency: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Human Foods Program
rules.title: Export certificates for soft drinks, bottled water and vinegar. FDA does not require one to export food, but many buyers do: the exporter applies online in HFP eCATS for a Certificate to a Foreign Government (food that meets U.S. law) or a Certificate of Exportability (export-only food).

citations.label: FDA: online applications for food export certificates

rules.title: Russia and Belarus "luxury goods" licence: beer (2203.00), wine (2204), undenatured ethanol (2207.10), whiskies, vodka, gin, rum, brandy, liqueurs and other spirits (2208) are on the BIS luxury-goods list, so exporting them to Russia or Belarus needs a Commerce licence, which BIS generally denies (15 CFR 746.8(a)(7) and Supplement No. 5 to Part 746).

groups.label: Mineral and aerated water, ice and snow (unsweetened)
groups.note: Bottled water is food under FDA rules. Nothing beyond the five steps unless the buyer asks for an FDA export certificate.

groups.label: Soft drinks, flavored water, energy drinks and other non-alcoholic beverages (incl. non-alcoholic beer)
groups.note: Soft drinks, energy drinks and non-alcoholic beer (0.5% alcohol or less) are FDA-regulated foods, not TTB products. An FDA export certificate when the buyer asks for one.

groups.label: Beer made from malt
groups.note: Beer leaves the brewery tax-free on a TTB F 5130.12 notice, or earns excise drawback if already taxpaid. Some buyers want a TTB certificate of free sale or health.

groups.label: Wine of fresh grapes (still and sparkling) and grape must
groups.note: Wine leaves bond tax-free on TTB F 5100.11. Every lot shipped to the EU needs the EU simplified export certificate or a VI-1 form; China and other APEC buyers take a TTB wine certificate. TTB’s wine labeling rules do not apply to wine exported in bond (27 CFR 4.80), so the label follows the buyer’s rules.

groups.label: Vermouth and other flavored wine
groups.note: Vermouth and flavored wine follow the wine rules: tax-free removal or drawback, and a TTB certificate where the buyer asks.

groups.label: Cider, perry, mead, sake and other fermented beverages
groups.note: Cider, mead and sake are taxed as wine and follow the wine rules: tax-free removal or drawback, and a TTB certificate where the buyer asks.

groups.label: Ethyl alcohol (undenatured 80%+ and denatured), incl. fuel ethanol
groups.note: Undenatured ethanol is distilled spirits for TTB, so it can leave a plant tax-free for export on TTB F 5100.11. Fuel ethanol exporters must retire RINs for the volume they export, and undenatured ethanol (2207.10) needs a BIS licence for Russia or Belarus.

groups.label: Spirits, liqueurs and other spirituous beverages (whisky, vodka, gin, rum, tequila, brandy)
groups.note: Bourbon and other spirits leave bond tax-free on TTB F 5100.11, or earn excise drawback if taxpaid. Exporters other than the distillery need a TTB basic permit. Many buyers want TTB F 5110.58 (origin and age) or F 5110.42 (bourbon authenticity).

groups.label: Vinegar
groups.note: Vinegar is an FDA-regulated food. An FDA export certificate when the buyer asks for one.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Ship ethanol to the UK inside the duty-free U.S. quota
savings.saves: The UK’s £16 per hectoliter duty on undenatured ethanol (£8.50 on denatured).
savings.appliesTo: U.S.-origin ethanol of heading 2207 imported into the UK, up to 1.4 billion liters per calendar year (quota 05.9750).
savings.document: The UK importer claims quota 05.9750 on the customs declaration with proof that the ethanol originates in the U.S.
savings.caveat: First come, first served: about 100.6 million liters of the 2026 quota were left on November 13, 2026. A new 1.4 billion liters opens on January 1, 2027.

citations.label: gov.uk: Update on the UK-US EPD

savings.title: Use the EU’s duty-free quota for U.S. soft drinks
savings.saves: The EU’s 9.6% duty on sweetened or flavored waters, non-alcoholic beer and other soft drinks.
savings.appliesTo: U.S.-origin goods of CN 2202 10 00, 2202 91 00 and 2202 99 19, up to 20,000 tonnes per 12-month period from July 1, 2026 (quota 09.9017).
savings.document: The EU importer declares preference code 320 for the quota with document code U190 (proof of non-preferential U.S. origin).
savings.caveat: First come, first served. Dairy-based drinks (2202 99 91–99) are not covered.

citations.label: Access2Markets: EU duties on U.S. goods from July 1, 2026

savings.title: Have your Chinese buyer use China’s tariff exclusion process
savings.saves: China’s 2018–19 Section 301 counter-tariffs: 25% on U.S. whiskey, other spirits, bottled wine, beer, ethanol, water and vinegar, and 27.5% on most soft drinks.
savings.appliesTo: U.S. Chapter 22 goods imported into China by a buyer whose exclusion covers them.
savings.document: The Chinese importer applies under China’s market-based exclusion process; the U.S. exporter supplies the product and origin details.
savings.caveat: Exclusions are valid until December 31, 2026, with no extension announced. They do not remove China’s extra 10% on all U.S. goods or its 15% 2018 counter-tariff on wine and denatured ethanol.

citations.label: White House fact sheet on the U.S.–China deal (Nov 1, 2025)

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
